body.text: Project accounting is a granular method of tracking budgets, labor hours, supplies, and contractor costs for each discrete project. For U.S. businesses claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41, it establishes the IRS-required nexus linking qualified research expenses to specific business components, strengthening substantiation and reducing audit disallowance risk.
Executive Summary: Project Accounting as the Foundation of R&D Credit Nexus

Project Accounting (PA) is a granular financial management and tracking discipline that records, monitors, and analyzes comprehensive financial data—specifically budgets, direct and indirect costs, resource utilization, cost behavior, and revenue—at the level of each discrete, individualized project. Whereas traditional financial accounting aggregates revenues and expenditures across an entire legal entity or broad organizational department over continuous, recurring fiscal periods, Project Accounting is bounded by the temporary, finite lifecycle of a single initiative from its inception date through milestone execution to account close-out. In professional services, software engineering, and technical hardware development environments, this financial architecture captures internal labor costs (derived from actual hours logged against specific tasks multiplied by individual employee hourly labor rates), external vendor and subcontractor expenditures, material requisitions, and budget-to-actual variances tied directly to defined deliverables.

Within the regulatory framework of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), which governs the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit—Project Accounting shifts from an internal operational control mechanism to a foundational tax compliance safeguard. Its primary regulatory function is establishing and substantiating "nexus": the verifiable financial and causal linkage connecting specific Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) recorded in the taxpayer's accounting ledgers to the corresponding Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) performed on an eligible business component.

The necessity of Project Accounting stems directly from examination standards enforced by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). In its Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG): Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41, the IRS defines the "nexus problem" as the inability to connect specific research projects and underlying technical activities to the claimed qualified expenses, noting that studies lacking this accounting-to-activity relationship fail to establish nexus and are consequently not auditable. The IRS RCCATG explicitly identifies project-based accounting as the accounting methodology that "generally establishes the required nexus between qualified activities and their related costs" because it captures research expenditures directly at the "business component" level. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation (Treas. Reg.) § 1.41-4(b)(1), taxpayers must apply the statutory four-part qualification test separately to each discrete business component. By tagging employee labor hours, consumable supply invoices, computer rental outlays, and third-party research contracts contemporaneously to a specific project code that maps to a defined business component, Project Accounting aligns the enterprise's financial data structure with the statutory unit of federal tax compliance. Consequently, this accounting structure isolates eligible QREs from non-qualifying General and Administrative (G&A) overhead, routine post-production maintenance, commercial production runs, and depreciable capital expenditures at the point of transaction entry, mitigating the risk of credit disallowance during IRS examinations.
Defining Project Accounting in an IRC Section 41 Context
Granular Mechanics of Project Accounting Versus Financial Accounting

As industry project-management literature (such as Productive.io, Rocketlane, and Scoro) and management accounting standards detail, Project Accounting operates as a micro-level financial tracking and control system designed to measure the cost behavior, milestone progression, resource efficiency, and financial viability of individual undertakings. Its core operational functions encompass establishing baseline project cost estimates and budgets, tracking internal labor through task-specific time logs multiplied by individualized hourly compensation rates, recording external vendor and subcontractor outlays, monitoring real-time budget-to-actual variances, separating direct from indirect and fixed from variable costs, and aligning revenue recognition with project delivery milestones and applicable accrual or cash accounting standards.

Traditional General Ledger (GL) financial accounting and Project Accounting serve fundamentally different analytical, managerial, and regulatory objectives. Financial accounting aggregates transactions into broad, entity-wide functional classifications—such as "Engineering Salaries," "Office and Lab Supplies," or "Outside Professional Services"—measured across standardized, recurring fiscal periods (monthly, quarterly, and annual cycles) to produce consolidated income statements and balance sheets for macro-level financial reporting. While sufficient for evaluating entity-wide financial stability and solvency, macro-level aggregation obscures the underlying technical purpose and deliverable association of individual expenditures. Project Accounting disaggregates those macro balances into project-specific sub-ledgers defined by project start and close-out dates, deliverable hierarchies, and granular task codes, enabling project managers, financial controllers, and tax professionals to evaluate resource deployment at the individual deliverable or sub-component level.

body.text: Aligning Financial Architecture with the Statutory Business Component

Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1), the qualification criteria for research activities must be applied separately with respect to each discrete "business component" of the taxpayer. IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) defines a "business component" as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Furthermore, IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) establishes a special plant-process rule mandating that any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component must be treated as a separate business component distinct from the product being produced. Because the statute mandates qualification testing and expenditure tracing at the discrete business component level, an accounting system that only records expenses at the legal entity or departmental cost-center level creates a fundamental structural mismatch between financial records and federal tax law.

Moreover, when an overall product, process, or software initiative fails to satisfy the statutory four-part test in its entirety, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) requires application of the "shrinking-back" rule. Under the shrink-back rule, the four-part qualification test is first applied at the level of the discrete business component; if all requirements are not met at that primary level, the test is applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention, continuing progressively downward until either a qualifying subset of elements is reached or the most basic element of the business component is reached and fails to satisfy the test. As tax advisory analyses following Little Sandy Coal note, tax teams should ensure that each business component is "shrink-back ready" so that the scope of any challenged component can be narrowed to a qualifying subset without losing the underlying claim. A Project Accounting system structured with hierarchical project and sub-task codes allows a taxpayer to isolate the cost of a qualifying sub-component element, whereas a monolithic departmental ledger cannot separate subset costs from non-qualifying work.

When taxpayers rely solely on standard financial accounting, preparing an R&D tax credit claim requires retrospective cost reconstruction—typically involving year-end interviews, questionnaires, or management surveys to estimate what fraction of a department's payroll and supply budget supported qualified research. By contrast, configuring Project Accounting so that each project code corresponds to a defined business component embeds tax compliance directly into daily accounting operations. Every time entry, material requisition, and contractor invoice generates a contemporaneous, system-dated transactional record tied to a specific business component, satisfying both the nexus standard of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide and the permanent recordkeeping mandates of IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d).
Regulatory Framework and R&D Tax Credit Fundamentals
Statutory Categories of Qualified Research Expenses Under IRC § 41(b)

IRC § 41(a) provides a credit against federal income tax for incremental Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) paid or incurred by a taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business (including start-up ventures meeting the principal-purpose test of IRC § 41(b)(4) for in-house research expenses). Taxpayers compute the credit either under the regular credit method of IRC § 41(a)(1)—equal to 20% of the excess of current-year QREs over a statutory base amount—or under the elective Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method of IRC § 41(c)(4) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-8. Under IRC § 41(b)(1), total QREs are defined as the sum of "in-house research expenses" (IRC § 41(b)(2)) and "contract research expenses" (IRC § 41(b)(3)). As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Qualified Research Expenses emphasizes, if an expense is not explicitly set forth in IRC § 41(b), a taxpayer cannot claim it as a QRE, requiring Project Accounting systems to segregate qualifying outlays from non-qualifying operational costs at the transaction level.

The first and largest statutory category is in-house employee wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and § 41(b)(2)(B), which covers taxable wages paid or incurred to an employee for performing "qualified services." Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), "wages" has the meaning given by IRC § 3401(a)—consisting of all taxable wages subject to withholding as reported on Form W-2, including bonuses and stock option redemptions (included in the year the option is exercised, provided the underlying work performed during the grant year constituted a qualified service), but excluding amounts not subject to withholding (such as non-taxed income or certain fringe benefits) as well as any wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Tax Credit under IRC § 51(a) (IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)). (For self-employed individuals and owner-employees within the meaning of IRC § 401(c)(1), IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii) includes the individual's earned income as defined in IRC § 401(c)(2).) Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), qualified services are statutorily limited to three specific functional roles:

items: Engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1));
Engaging in the direct supervision—meaning immediate, first-line management—of qualified research (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)); and
Engaging in the direct support of persons engaging in the actual conduct or direct supervision of qualified research (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)).

body.text: Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), employee wages are normally included in QREs in exact proportion to the ratio of hours spent performing qualified services relative to total hours worked during the taxable year (for example, an engineer earning $150,000 who logs 60% of hours to qualified research yields $90,000 in qualifying wage QREs and $60,000 in excluded wages), unless the employee reaches the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), in which case 100% ($150,000) of the employee's wages qualify.

The second statutory category comprises consumed supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C), defined as any tangible property used or consumed directly in the conduct of qualified research—such as raw materials or pilot-model inputs expended to fabricate and test experimental prototypes—which are eligible at a 100% inclusion rate. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(i)–(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b), the term "supplies" explicitly excludes: (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) any property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, such as capital laboratory equipment, machinery, or research facilities, all of which carry a 0% QRE inclusion rate. Furthermore, in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Second Circuit rejected the taxpayer's claim that raw materials used to produce commercial goods for sale—costs the taxpayer would have incurred whether or not it conducted process research on the manufacturing line—were supplies "used in the conduct of qualified research" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Conversely, as practitioner analyses of George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, report, the Tax Court validated that tangible inputs (such as feed and trial costs for experimental flocks) are includable as pilot-model supply QREs where variables under review cannot be tested without them, and clarified that supply claims are independent of whether wage QREs are claimed on the same experiment.

The third category consists of contract research expenses (CRE) under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A), 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research performed on behalf of the taxpayer is eligible as a QRE. Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C)(i)–(ii), this statutory inclusion rate increases to 75% for amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to a "qualified research consortium"—defined as a tax-exempt organization described in IRC § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) that is organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research and is not a private foundation—for qualified research conducted on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers. Additionally, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D), the statutory inclusion rate increases to 100% for amounts paid or incurred to an eligible small business, an institution of higher education (as defined in IRC § 3304(f)), or a federal laboratory for qualified energy research. To qualify as contract research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), payment must be made pursuant to an agreement that satisfies three conditions: (1) it is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research; (2) it provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer (meaning the taxpayer has a right to the research results, even if non-exclusive); and (3) it requires the taxpayer to bear the economic risk of the expense even if the research is not successful. Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B), any prepaid contract research expense attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of the taxable year is treated as paid or incurred only during the period in which the qualified research is actually conducted.

Across all categories, overhead and indirect expenditures—including General and Administrative (G&A) expenses, travel, meals, entertainment, telephone expenses of researchers, relocation or lease expenses, professional dues, royalty or license fees, general janitorial services, and accounting for non-research operations—are statutorily ineligible (0% inclusion), necessitating dedicated General Ledger sub-accounts and project codes to prevent commingling.
The Four-Part Test for Qualified Research Activities Under IRC § 41(d)

Before any expenditure captured in a Project Accounting system can be claimed as a QRE, the underlying technical initiative must satisfy four concurrent statutory tests set forth in IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a), while avoiding the statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4):

items: The Section 174 / 174A Expense & Elimination of Uncertainty Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)): Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the research must be an activity with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (historically and in cross-referenced regulations, IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3) and § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent R&D costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and are intended at the outset of the initiative to discover information that would eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that component.

The Technological in Nature Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)): Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of discovering it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under final regulations (Treasury Decision 9104), discovering technological information does not require the taxpayer to obtain knowledge that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field.

The Business Component & Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)): Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Concurrently, under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(A), the activity must be conducted for a "qualified purpose"—specifically, to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Conversely, under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), activities relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors are statutorily excluded from qualified purposes.

The Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain at the outset of the taxpayer's research activities—involving the identification of technical uncertainty, the formulation and evaluation of design alternatives or hypotheses, modeling, simulation, prototyping, or systematic trial and error. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) (which is distinct from the wage "substantially all" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)) is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

body.text: In addition to satisfying the four-part test, a project must not fall within the statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4), which disqualify research conducted after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component, duplication of an existing business component, efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research or promotions, routine data collection, routine quality-control testing or inspection, foreign research conducted outside the United States (or Puerto Rico and U.S. possessions), and funded research.

From an analytical standpoint, the four-part test establishes qualitative technical eligibility, while Project Accounting establishes quantitative financial capture. Neither element suffices in isolation. A comprehensive engineering narrative demonstrating systematic experimentation cannot sustain a tax credit if the accounting system cannot isolate the specific labor, supply, and contractor costs expended on that experiment. Furthermore, because Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) measures the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold on a cost or reasonable basis per business component, a Project Accounting system that tracks costs by sub-task enables the taxpayer to substantiate that at least 80% of the project's research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation. Conversely, meticulous project time logs yield zero tax benefit if the project code corresponds to routine maintenance or cosmetic updates that fail the four-part test, requiring tight cross-functional alignment wherein the technical team's definition of an eligible business component governs the finance team's project coding structure.
The Nexus Mandate, Audit Risk Mitigation, and Contemporaneous Substantiation
Establishing Nexus Under the IRS Audit Techniques Guide

In IRS examinations of R&D tax credit claims, the primary point of dispute is frequently the taxpayer's inability to establish a verifiable "nexus" linking accounting records (QREs) to qualified technical activities (QRAs) at the business component level. The IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) repeatedly highlights examiner concerns regarding claims that exhibit a "lack of nexus" between identified business components and pooled departmental expenditures, instructing examining agents that studies failing to support the relationship between accounting records and research activities are not auditable.

When evaluating taxpayer accounting systems, the IRS RCCATG explicitly favors project-based accounting because it captures research costs directly at the business component level, thereby establishing the required direct nexus between QRAs and QREs. Indeed, the RCCATG advises IRS examiners that if a taxpayer maintained a project accounting methodology during the tax year but chose not to use it in claiming the research credit, examiners should inquire why it was not used, as project-based accounting may be the best methodology for auditing the claim. Under a Project Accounting regime, an IRS examiner can trace any dollar claimed on Form 6765 backward through an unbroken evidentiary trail: from the tax return schedule to the General Ledger project code, to the individual employee's approved digital timesheet or vendor invoice, and finally to the contemporaneous technical documentation demonstrating that the specific business component satisfied the four-part test.
Deficiencies of Cost Center and Hybrid Accounting Systems

Taxpayers lacking Project Accounting typically rely on either cost center accounting or hybrid estimation approaches, both of which expose R&D tax credit claims to severe audit disallowance risk. Cost center accounting organizes expenditures by broad organizational unit or department (for example, "Engineering Department"), which inherently commingles qualified research costs with non-qualified operational activities such as routine maintenance, production support, client administration, and legacy bug fixing.

Hybrid and top-down estimation approaches attempt to bridge this structural gap by combining available cost center payroll or general ledger totals with retrospective percentage estimates derived from manager recollections, Subject Matter Expert (SME) interviews, or year-end questionnaires. As documented in the IRS RCCATG, a common hybrid nexus failure occurs when W-2 wages are captured by cost center and multiplied by a "qualified percentage" applied either to individual employee wages or as a single percentage across total department wage costs, often relying on SMEs whose representations lack measurable corroborative records. The IRS RCCATG explicitly instructs examining agents that when QREs captured via a cost center or hybrid approach cannot be traced to a specific business component, disallowance of part or all of the cost center may be appropriate if any of the following four conditions exist:

items: All or part of the activities undertaken in the cost center did not involve qualified research activities;
All or part of the expenses claimed in the cost center as QREs were not qualified research expenses;
The taxpayer's sole basis for substantiating qualified activities in the cost center was estimates; or
The basis for allocating qualified or non-qualified activities and expenses is arbitrary.

body.text: In the first scenario, a company incurs $1,000,000 in departmental expenditures. Under a standard General Ledger view, the $1,000,000 appears as an opaque "Black Box" split into $800,000 of "Total Engineering Salaries" and $200,000 of "Supplies & Cloud Costs," yielding $0 in directly substantiated QREs and forcing reliance on legally vulnerable estimates (High Audit Risk). When tracked through Project Accounting, that identical $1,000,000 spend is disaggregated by activity: $350,000 for Project A (AI Algorithm — Qualifying), $150,000 for Project B (New UI — Qualifying), $300,000 for Legacy Maintenance (Non-Qualifying), $100,000 for Admin/PTO (Non-Qualifying), and $100,000 for Cloud Hosting (Non-Qualifying), isolating $500,000 ($350,000 + $150,000) in fully substantiated QREs with Low Audit Risk. In the second scenario ("TechNova Corp"), an enterprise spends $1,200,000 on software engineering salaries coded to a single "Salaries" GL account without time tracking. A top-down manager estimate assuming "50% of time on R&D" yields $600,000 in QREs ($1,200,000 × 50%) but carries High Audit Risk due to the absence of contemporaneous nexus. Replacing that estimate with job-code Project Accounting uncovers $725,000 in substantiated QREs—identifying $125,000 in previously hidden R&D time while establishing a defensible IRS audit trail.
Contemporaneous Documentation and Form 6765 Reporting Mandates

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) (promulgated under T.D. 9104), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must "retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit," cross-referencing the general record-retention rules of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a), which require organizations to keep permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, or credits. While Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) does not prescribe a single universal recordkeeping format, both IRS examination guidelines and federal courts place premium evidentiary weight on contemporaneous documentation—records generated in the ordinary course of business at the time the research activity and expenditure occur, rather than reconstructed years later during an audit.
Furthermore, two major IRS administrative and reporting developments have elevated project-level accounting from a best practice into a vital compliance requirement:

items: IRS Research Credit Refund Claim Perfection Requirements (Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)): Under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and IRS administrative guidance (IR-2021-203, as modified by the IRS update effective June 18, 2024), taxpayers submitting an amended return or refund claim that includes an IRC § 41 research credit must provide three core project-level disclosures at the time of filing:
Identify all business components to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that tax year;
For each business component, describe all research activities performed; and

Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. (Although the June 18, 2024 update waived the requirement at initial filing to provide the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover, the IRS may still request those records during an examination.) Federal decisions—including Harper (847 F. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021)) and Premier Tech, Inc. (No. 2:20-cv-890 (D. Utah July 15, 2022))—highlight the procedural risks refund claims face when they lack project-level details.

Revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) and Mandatory Section G Disclosures: Under the revised Form 6765 and its official IRS Instructions (Rev. January 2025 / December 2025), the IRS introduced Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary) and Section G (Business Component Information). While Section G was optional for tax years beginning before 2026, Section G is mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (on or after January 1, 2026) unless the filer qualifies for one of two exceptions:

Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Credit Election: The filer is a Qualified Small Business under IRC § 41(h)(3) (a corporation, partnership, or sole proprietorship with under $5,000,000 in gross receipts for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with that tax year) and checks the box on Form 6765 (Line 33a) to claim up to $500,000 of its research credit as a payroll tax credit on Form 8974; or

Small-Filer Exception: The filer reports controlled-group QREs of $1,500,000 or less (Line 48), has average annual gross receipts of $50,000,000 or less (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3)) for the three preceding tax years, and claims the research credit on an original return.

body.text: For all filers required to complete Section G on Form 6765, the instructions enforce the "80%/Top 50" Business Component Reporting Rule: taxpayers must report by business component a minimum of 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components, with any remaining business components reported in aggregate as "Aggregate Business Components." For each itemized business component, Section G requires reporting the component type and breaking out qualified employee wages, supplies, computer rental costs, and applicable contract research expenses attributable to that component. Without an active Project Accounting framework logging wages, supplies, and contractor invoices by business component throughout the fiscal year, compiling these mandatory disclosures accurately is operationally burdensome and vulnerable to audit challenge.
Operationalizing Project Accounting Across QRE Categories: Rules, Precedents, and Hypothetical Worked Examples
Substantiating Qualified Wages, the "Substantially All" Rule, and Judicial Precedent

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and IRS examination guidelines, employee compensation is evaluated strictly on the nature of the services actually performed by the individual during the taxable year, irrespective of job descriptions, titles, or academic credentials. Qualified services comprise three statutory categories:

items: Engaging in Qualified Research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)): The actual conduct of qualified research, such as a scientist conducting laboratory experiments or a developer writing experimental code.

Direct Supervision of Qualified Research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)): The immediate, first-line management of qualified research, such as a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist (unless personally performing actual qualified research or first-line supervision).

Direct Support of Qualified Research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)): Services in the direct support of either persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising such research—such as a machinist machining a part for an experimental model, a lab worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, or a secretary typing laboratory result reports.

body.text: Administrative tasks, general janitorial work, marketing collateral preparation, sales meetings, payroll personnel preparing checks, accountants accounting for research expenses, and officers supervising financial or personnel matters are strictly excluded from QREs regardless of whether those employees are assigned to the research department.
Regulatory Mechanics of the "Substantially All" Rule

Under the flush language of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all" of the services performed by an individual for the taxpayer during a taxable year consist of qualified services (meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii)), then all (100%) of the services performed by that individual for the taxpayer during the taxable year are treated as qualified services. Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) defines "substantially all" quantitatively: the threshold is satisfied only if 80% or more of the employee's wages during the taxable year (determined by comparing actual hours spent performing qualified services to total hours worked) are attributable to qualified services.
Case Law Precedents on Time Allocation and Corroboration
Judicial decisions underscore the hazards of claiming wage QREs without project-level substantiation and illustrate the strict boundaries of judicial estimation.

In Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235 (1994), the U.S. Tax Court examined research credit claims for Light Sculpting Co., a sole proprietorship formed in 1985 by Dr. Efrem V. Fudim (an inventor holding a doctorate from the Institute of Control Sciences of the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences) to research a "rapid modeling" (rapid prototyping) process using photopolymers and ultraviolet light. During 1986, 1987, and 1988, Dr. Fudim claimed research credits based on his own self-employment income, wages paid in 1987 to his wife, Margarita L. Fudim, and wages paid in 1986, 1987, and 1988 to his daughter, Natalia Fudim.

items: Dr. Efrem V. Fudim (Petitioner / Husband): Although Dr. Fudim had no contemporaneous time logs at trial (claiming he discarded them after an initial audit), the record included 39 patents and 38 scientific papers prior to 1985, two U.S. patents issued in June 1988 and January 1989 on the rapid modeling process, articles in scientific and popular publications featuring Light Sculpting Co., and evidence that his outside consulting for Sundstrand (at an average of $1,500 per day) occupied only approximately 12 days in 1986, 36 days in 1987, and 43 days in 1988. Estimating his time under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Tax Court held that Dr. Fudim spent more than 80% of his working time at Light Sculpting Co. during 1986, 1987, and 1988 engaged in qualified research services, qualifying all (100%) of his Light Sculpting time under the "substantially all" rule.

Margarita L. Fudim (Wife): Mrs. Margarita L. Fudim held a mechanical engineering degree from the Moscow Institute of Chemical Machine Building and worked full-time as a computer programmer at Pansophic Systems. From May through December 1987, she worked 600 hours part-time for Light Sculpting Co. at $16.00 per hour (totaling $9,600 in wages), assisting her husband with designing, drafting, and performing experiments. Given her technical qualifications and direct experimental role, the Tax Court held under Cohan that Margarita L. Fudim spent at least 80% of her time in 1987 engaged in qualified services, qualifying her 1987 wages ($9,600) for inclusion in the research credit computation.

Natalia Fudim (Daughter): Natalia Fudim worked part-time at Light Sculpting Co. during 1986, 1987, and 1988 at wages between $6.40 and $8.00 per hour, earning $4,800 in 1986, $5,900 in 1987, and $9,859 in 1988. The Tax Court completely disallowed any research credit based on the wages paid to Natalia Fudim, noting that the record failed to reveal her age, formal training, or level of technical expertise, and that the petitioner failed to present any concrete evidence showing what specific services Natalia actually rendered. Consequently, her hours could not be estimated under the Cohan rule.

body.text: Under Cohan, if a taxpayer establishes that a deductible or creditable expense was incurred but cannot substantiate the exact amount, the court may approximate the amount, "bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making." However, as established in Vanicek v. Commissioner, 85 T.C. 731, 742–43 (1985), and Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d at 567, for the Cohan rule to apply, a reasonable evidentiary basis must exist in the record upon which an estimate can be made.

In Shami, the corporate taxpayer (Farouk Systems, Inc., a hair-care product manufacturer) claimed research credits in which 80% of total claimed QREs consisted of the wages of its Chief Executive Officer (CEO, Farouk Shami) and Executive Vice President (EVP), asserting that both executives satisfied the 80% "substantially all" rule. Neither executive had formal education or training in engineering or chemistry, and the taxpayer failed to produce any documentation or corroborative records proving their involvement or allocated time in research activities. The Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit rejected the retroactive, uncorroborated percentage estimates and refused to invoke Cohan. Similarly, in Moore v. Commissioner, T.C., the Tax Court emphasized that "Section 41(d) requires us to walk by sight, not by faith," holding that the taxpayer bears the burden to document that the activities accounted for by nonproduction wages were elements of a process of experimentation and that "documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary," while in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, the court again penalized broad, aggressive estimates. Project Accounting directly satisfies the evidentiary threshold demanded by Fudim, Cohan, Shami, Moore, and George by generating manager-approved digital timesheets, qualitative technical activity notes, and project-linked payroll records contemporaneously.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Employee Wage Allocation and the 80% Threshold

To demonstrate how Project Accounting operationalizes IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), consider two hypothetical software engineers at a technology firm, each earning $150,000 in annual Form W-2 Box 1 taxable wages across a 2,000-hour work year, equating to an hourly compensation rate of $75/hour ($150,000 / 2,000 hours = $75/hour).

In the first hypothetical case, Developer A works on a new security feature (an eligible business component) and logs 1,600 hours (80% of total annual time) in the Project Accounting time-tracking system under Project Code PROJ-SEC-01 for writing experimental encryption code and conducting systematic testing to resolve performance uncertainty (a qualifying QRA). Developer A logs the remaining 400 hours (20% of total annual time) to Cost Code ADMIN-MKT for attending sales meetings and developing marketing collateral (Non-QRA). Multiplying logged hours by the $75/hour labor rate yields direct project labor of $120,000 ($75/hour × 1,600 hours) for QRAs and $30,000 ($75/hour × 400 hours) for Non-QRAs. However, because Developer A's qualified service ratio is 1,600 / 2,000 = 80%, which meets the 80% "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), 100% of Developer A's annual taxable wages ($150,000) qualify as wage QREs, capturing an additional $30,000 statutory step-up.

In the second hypothetical case, Engineer B logs 1,200 hours (60% of total annual time) to Project Code PROJ-ALGO-02 ("New Algorithm Development" — Qualifying QRA) and 800 hours (40% of total annual time) to Project Code MAINT-LEG-01 ("Legacy System Maintenance" — Non-Qualifying). Multiplying the logged hours by the $75/hour labor rate yields $90,000 ($75/hour × 1,200 hours) in direct QRA labor and $60,000 ($75/hour × 800 hours) in non-qualifying maintenance labor. Because Engineer B's qualified service ratio is 1,200 / 2,000 = 60%, which falls below the 80% regulatory cliff of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), only the exact project-tracked qualifying portion ($90,000) is eligible as a wage QRE, while the $60,000 charged to legacy maintenance is strictly excluded.
Tracking Consumed Supplies and Contract Research Expenses

Project Accounting applies identical transactional rigor to non-wage expenditures under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and IRC § 41(b)(3). For supply QREs (IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)), purchase orders and vendor invoices for tangible materials consumed directly in fabricating and testing prototypes must be coded to the corresponding Business Component Project ID at procurement, separating 100%-eligible consumable materials from excluded capital equipment (property of a character subject to depreciation under IRC § 167 and excluded under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii)), routine commercial production supplies (excluded under Union Carbide), and general office supplies.

For contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)), third-party research agreements, purchase orders, and vendor invoices must likewise be coded to the specific R&D Project ID to verify the scope of research performed on behalf of the taxpayer (and confirm compliance with the three-part agreement test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) and the prepaid research timing rule of IRC § 41(b)(3)(B)) before applying the statutory 65% limitation (IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)) for standard third-party contractors, the 75% limitation (IRC § 41(b)(3)(C)) for payments to a qualified research consortium, or the 100% inclusion rate (IRC § 41(b)(3)(D)) for eligible energy research. Where a vendor invoice includes both qualified developer services and non-qualified post-production release support services, the invoice must be broken out by project task code so only the portion attributable to qualified research is included in the 65% computation.
Hypothetical Worked Example 2: Non-Wage QRE Segregation and Statutory Haircuts

Consider a hypothetical hardware manufacturer that incurs $270,000 in gross external vendor outlays during the tax year while developing an experimental sensor module (Project ID: SENS-X1). Through Project Accounting invoice coding and manager approval, the $270,000 gross spend is segregated into four distinct General Ledger sub-accounts:

items: $50,000 for raw materials consumed in fabricating and destructively testing sensor prototypes (Account 5110-RD-SUP);
$80,000 for an oscilloscope and environmental test chamber (depreciable capital equipment posted to Account 1500-CAP-EQUIP);
$100,000 paid to an independent engineering firm for prototype testing (Account 5120-RD-CRE); and
$40,000 paid to a qualified research consortium for specialized material testing (Account 5125-RD-CON).

body.text: Applying the statutory inclusion rules of IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and § 41(b)(3) yields $50,000 × 100% = $50,000, $80,000 × 0% = $0, $100,000 × 65% = $65,000, and $40,000 × 75% = $30,000, resulting in a total substantiated non-wage QRE claim of $50,000 + $0 + $65,000 + $30,000 = $145,000 out of the $270,000 gross expenditure.

body.text: Systems Integration and Chart of Accounts Governance
Chart of Accounts Strategy and Dimensional Financial Coding

A defensible R&D tax credit architecture begins in the enterprise General Ledger (GL) and Chart of Accounts (COA). Rather than posting all technical expenditures into monolithic accounts, financial leadership should establish dedicated, high-level R&D expense accounts and sub-accounts corresponding to the statutory QRE categories—specifically R&D Salaries and Wages, R&D Supplies and Materials, and R&D Contract Services, kept distinct from R&D Overhead sub-accounts that record non-qualifying indirect costs such as lab space rent, utilities, or equipment depreciation.

Within modern Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and accounting platforms—such as QuickBooks (using Classes, Locations, and Departments), NetSuite (using Departments, Classes, Locations, Subsidiaries, and Custom Segments), or Xero (using Tracking Categories)—taxpayers can deploy dimensional accounting. As technical integration documentation from Apideck notes, each platform enforces specific dimensional rules: QuickBooks Online requires users to explicitly enable "Track classes" and "Track locations" in company settings (while Intuit Enterprise Suite supports up to 20 custom dimensions); NetSuite OneWorld requires a valid subsidiary_id on multi-entity transactions and supports custom segments; and Xero limits each organization to two active Tracking Categories, requiring careful upfront planning so one category captures the R&D Project / Business Component and the second captures the Department or Activity type.

Each transaction posted to an R&D GL account is assigned a mandatory dimensional tag representing the specific Business Component or Project ID (for example, "Project Alpha - Algorithm Design"), alongside a task classification separating "New Development" from "Maintenance" and "Admin." To prevent misclassifications before they enter the General Ledger, organizations should enforce a formal R&D expense approval workflow wherein a project manager or technical lead verifies that every supply purchase invoice or third-party contract expense directly supports an approved R&D business component before the transaction is posted with an R&D GL code. Additionally, as startup accounting guidance from Kruze Consulting highlights, when booking the resulting R&D tax credit on the financial statements, accrual accounting uses an R&D Tax Credit Receivable asset account on the balance sheet and an R&D Tax Credit Income account on the income statement (reducing the receivable each quarter as payroll tax offsets are applied), avoiding the financial modeling distortions caused by booking a lump-sum cash-basis reduction to payroll tax expense.
Three-Tier Technology Stack Integration for Contemporaneous Capture

As the IRS increasingly utilizes automated data analytics to examine complex tax claims, manual spreadsheets reconstructed at year-end present heightened audit exposure. Best-practice Project Accounting integrates three operational technology layers into a unified, high-transparency data pipeline:

items: Layer 1 — Project Management & Issue-Tracking Tools (Jira, GitHub, Asana): The first layer comprises project management and issue-tracking tools such as Jira and GitHub, which capture the granular technical workflow—sprint tickets, code commits, architectural specifications, and test outcomes—that substantiate the qualitative four-part test.

Layer 2 — Dedicated Time-Tracking Software (My Hours, ClickTime): The second layer consists of dedicated time-tracking software such as My Hours and ClickTime, which provide structured project codes and sub-task categories (such as "prototype development") against which technical personnel log hours contemporaneously along with qualitative activity descriptions. According to vendor documentation from ClickTime, its ClickTime AI feature can automatically map developer activity from Jira, Asana, and calendars into pre-defined QRE project and cost codes at the point of entry while preserving timestamped audit trails, approval workflows, and change histories. Similarly, vendor documentation from My Hours notes that its platform organizes R&D work into a three-tier hierarchy (Client Spaces, Projects, and Tasks), supports mandatory project/task fields and custom claimable vs. non-claimable tags, sends automated daily and weekly reminders, locks approved timesheets against subsequent edits, and allows uploading photos or files of vendor receipts and invoices directly to R&D tasks.

Layer 3 — Enterprise General Ledger & Payroll ERP Systems (QuickBooks, NetSuite, Xero, Sage Intacct): The third layer is the enterprise General Ledger and payroll ERP system, which ingests approved timesheets, automatically applies each employee's unique hourly labor rate to compute accumulated project labor costs, and links approved accounts payable invoices for supplies and contractors to the identical Project IDs.

body.text: Together, these integrated systems compile labor hours, supply costs, contractor invoices, and qualitative project narratives into an auditable package without disruptive retrospective reconstruction.
Implementation Strategy: Institutionalizing an "Always On" Compliance Culture

Transitioning from reactive, year-end claim reconstruction to proactive, audit-ready Project Accounting requires coordinated procedural, educational, and governance reforms. Foremost among these is establishing a formal, recurring "R&D housekeeping" cadence—such as a monthly or quarterly close schedule—integrated directly into existing operational workflows. At each monthly cutoff, technical personnel finalize timesheets within their project management or time-tracking software, technical leads review, approve, and lock time logs and qualitative activity notes, and the finance team exports payroll and accounts payable project ledgers to update the master QRE schedule. Including a brief standing agenda item on R&D activity logging during regular engineering team meetings minimizes friction and ensures continuous data completeness throughout the tax year.

Concurrently, organizations should conduct targeted internal training to bridge the operational divide between engineering teams and tax compliance. Employees involved in research and development must be trained on the statutory criteria of the IRC § 41(d) four-part test so they can accurately distinguish between routine bug fixing or post-production maintenance (ineligible) and systematic experimentation aimed at resolving technological uncertainty (eligible). Staff training should emphasize that qualitative notes attached to project time logs and tickets—documenting the specific technical uncertainty encountered, the hypotheses tested, and the results of failed or successful experiments—serve as primary tax substantiation, whereas vague or generic descriptions invite auditor disallowance. Finally, taxpayers should run mock Form 6765 reports prior to filing to confirm that the top 50 business components cover the required 80% of QREs under Section G, and engage specialized R&D tax practitioners to review and validate the entire Project Accounting architecture—from initial Chart of Accounts setup to the application of complex statutory rules such as the IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) "substantially all" threshold—ensuring that a complete, project-specific audit defense package is maintained contemporaneously.
